claims.claim: Every clause contains two parts: a subject, which names who or what the clause is about, and a predicate, which says something about that subject and is built around a verb.
The subject of a clause is usually a noun or pronoun, and the core word (the simple subject) is what the verb connects to; descriptive words and phrases around it form the complete subject.
A compound subject consists of two or more nouns or pronouns joined by a conjunction such as and, or, or nor, sharing one predicate.
A predicate can contain two or more verbs joined by a conjunction and sharing the same subject (a compound predicate), as with coordinated verb phrases.
Imperative sentences give a request, command, or instruction; the subject is not stated and is understood as the person addressed (you).
In interrogative sentences (questions), the subject commonly appears after an auxiliary verb, and restating the question as a statement reveals the subject.
Recognizing subjects and predicates helps writers diagnose incomplete sentences (fragments) and locate the true subject for agreement between subject and verb.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology for the two subject levels varies across references: some school-grammar texts teach 'simple subject' and 'complete subject' as standard terms, while other references, such as Writing for Success, describe the subject through the who-or-what test without naming the simple/complete split.
positions: Simple subject and complete subject are standard labels in many grammar courses.
Writing for Success defines the subject as the word telling who or what the sentence is about, usually a noun or pronoun, and illustrates compound subjects without using the term 'simple subject.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines both levels explicitly and grounds them in the who-or-what test and the noun-or-pronoun core described in the verified sources, so the labels and the underlying analysis agree with the sources used.

sourceRecords.title: Writing for Success — 2.1: Sentence Writing
sourceRecords.provider: Humanities LibreTexts (book by Scott McLean, originally University of Minnesota)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: defines the subject as who or what the sentence is about, states subjects are usually nouns or pronouns, defines compound subjects (two or more nouns or pronouns joined by and/or/nor), and covers action, linking, and helping verbs. Supports the who-or-what test, the simple/complete subject analysis, and the compound subject claim. The Saylor mirror (https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_writing-for-success/s06-01-sentence-writing.html) was also checked and matches.

sourceRecords.title: Language Foundations Handbook — Sentences: Sentence Forms
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: 'In a clause, the subject is the noun or pronoun that is "doing" the verb' and 'a clause is a group of words with a subject and a predicate.' Its compound-sentence example ('He is stretching and he is grooming himself') illustrates coordinated verb phrases, used to support the compound predicate concept. License not stated on the page; treated as reference-only.

sourceRecords.title: Language Foundations Handbook — Sentences: Sentence Types
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: defines imperative as a request, command, or instruction, with the example 'Enjoy that sunshine, Simba' (a command with no written subject), and interrogative as a question, with the example 'How does he twist like that?' (auxiliary before subject). Supports the command and question claims.

sourceRecords.title: Purdue OWL — Sentence Fragments
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: 'Fragments are incomplete sentences. Usually, fragments are pieces of sentences that have become disconnected from the main clause.' Supports the claim that recognizing subjects and predicates helps diagnose incomplete sentences.

sourceRecords.title: Purdue OWL — Subject/Verb Agreement
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: guidelines for making the subject and verb agree, including that expressions such as 'together with' do not change the subject. Cited only for the sibling-topic connection that locating the true subject precedes agreement decisions; agreement rules themselves belong to the subject-verb-agreement topic.
